name: gnucobol
desc: COBOL85-202x compiler supporting lots of dialect specific extensions
why: A COBOL compiler that lets you write and run the language still powering old banking and mainframe systems.

brief.what_it_is: GnuCOBOL is a free/libre COBOL compiler that produces native executables from COBOL source code. It is described as working on Linux, BSD, many proprietary Unixes, macOS, and Windows. The homepage lists support for 19 COBOL dialects, REPORT SECTION, SCREEN SECTION, FUNCTION-ID, C integration, and a COBOL 2014 Compiler Directing Facility feature set. The current release is 3.2, released 28 July 2023. The Homebrew package installs three executables: cob-config, cobc, and cobcrun.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a free/libre COBOL compiler for people who want to write and run COBOL outside proprietary toolchains. The page does not give a longer origin story. The page footer quotes the FSF's mission of software freedom, which frames the project's values.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internals. It says GnuCOBOL produces native executables from COBOL source, and it mentions GNU gdb support and an integrated IDE debugging feature. It does not describe the translation pipeline in detail.
brief.install_notes: The homepage links to downloads for GNU/Linux, BSDs, Windows, and MacOS, plus a SourceForge download and GNU ftp mirrors. It names no hardware, account, or runtime requirements. The 3.2 NEWS file and runtime.cfg are referenced for configuration of runtime file handling, and -std flags change dialect defaults. No first-run steps appear on the homepage.
brief.standout: It is a native-code COBOL compiler with a long dialect list and C integration, so you can mix COBOL with C. The project claims over 9740 NIST COBOL 85 tests passed, which is a concrete conformance claim. Most people meet COBOL only through mainframes, and this runs on ordinary desktops.
brief.status: Maintained as far as the homepage shows. The 3.2 release is dated 28 July 2023, and the page lists 3.1.2 (December 2020) and 3.1.rc-1 (June 2020) as earlier releases. The page calls 3.2 the best version for all users. I did not check the SourceForge or GitHub commit history, so I cannot confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not list licensing terms, though GNU project hosting implies a GPL-style license, and I did not verify that. The homepage gives no install commands and no list of known limitations. Platform support is described in general terms only. The homepage is a marketing and download page, so the feature claims could not be checked against the source here.
quotes: GnuCOBOL produces native executables from COBOL source code.
The current release, version 3.2, is the best version for all users.

judge.reason: GnuCOBOL makes a still-used legacy language runnable on ordinary machines, inviting a hands-on look at COBOL dialects and old mainframe-era programming.

entry.title: GnuCOBOL
entry.tldr: A free COBOL compiler that turns the language behind banks and mainframes into native executables on an ordinary laptop.
entry.deeper_look:
GnuCOBOL compiles COBOL source into native executables. Homebrew installs three tools: `cobc`, the compiler; `cobcrun`, which runs compiled modules; and `cob-config`, which reports the compiler and library settings you need when linking. The homepage says it runs on Linux, BSD, macOS, Windows and several proprietary Unixes.

COBOL is the language still running a large share of banking, insurance and government batch processing. Most developers never see it because it lives on mainframes behind proprietary toolchains. GnuCOBOL lets you write and run it at home. The homepage frames the project around software freedom, in the FSF's terms, and offers a free/libre alternative to those toolchains.

The homepage lists support for 19 COBOL dialects, switched with `-std` flags, along with REPORT SECTION, SCREEN SECTION, FUNCTION-ID and a COBOL 2014 Compiler Directing Facility feature set. It also supports C integration, so COBOL and C can be mixed in one program. The project claims more than 9740 passed NIST COBOL 85 tests, a concrete conformance figure.

The idea underneath is a language designed in about 1959 for business records, with fixed-point decimal data and column-oriented source. Writing even a small program shows how different the assumptions behind it are from modern languages.

entry.whats_unique: It is a native-code COBOL compiler with a long dialect list and C integration, and it runs on ordinary desktops instead of mainframes.
entry.caveats: The homepage gives no install commands or known limitations, and recent commit activity was not checked. The latest release it lists is 3.2, from July 2023.
